etymology: From Anselm (c. 1033–1109), an Italian monk who became Abbot of Bec and Archbishop of Canterbury; the name from the Germanic ans (god) and helm (helmet, protection).
biblical_def: Anselm of Canterbury was a medieval monk, abbot, and archbishop, one of the keenest minds of the age, whose chief labour was to give reasoned account of the faith he already believed—“faith seeking understanding.” The dictionary honours two of his enduring contributions. First, in his great work Cur Deus Homo (“Why God Became Man”) he set forth the satisfaction theory of the atonement: that sin is an infinite offence against the infinite majesty of God, that the debt could be paid by none but God yet must be paid by man, and that therefore the God-man alone could make satisfaction—a true forerunner of the Reformed doctrine of penal substitution, in which Christ bears the debt His people could never pay. Second, in the Proslogion he framed the ontological argument, reasoning from the very idea of God as “that than which nothing greater can be conceived” to His necessary existence. The dictionary receives these as honourable labours of a mind devoted to God, drawing out from Scripture and reason what the cross truly accomplished. Yet Anselm laboured within the medieval Roman church, and his piety was marked by its errors—a tender but mistaken devotion to the Virgin Mary, addressing prayers to her, and a sacramental and ecclesial framework that the Reformation would later test by the Word and find wanting in part. The dictionary applies its rule for figures outside the Reformed tradition: honour the genuine insight into the cross and the rigour of his thought, while naming his Marian devotion and Roman setting as the error of his age. The seed of substitution he planted, the Reformers brought to its full harvest.
webster_summary: Medieval Archbishop of Canterbury (c. 1033–1109); honoured for the satisfaction theory of the atonement in Cur Deus Homo (a forerunner of penal substitution) and the ontological argument, with his Marian devotion and Roman setting named as error.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The dictionary honours the genuine good in Anselm: a mind of rare power consecrated to God, who gave the church the satisfaction theory of the atonement in Cur Deus Homo. Reasoning that sin is an infinite offence against an infinite God, that the debt must be paid by man yet can be paid only by God, he concluded that the God-man alone could satisfy—a true forerunner of the Reformed doctrine of penal substitution, in which Christ bears the punishment His people deserved. His ontological argument likewise stands as a serious labour of faith seeking understanding. These the dictionary receives with gratitude as honourable history.

Yet Anselm was a man of the medieval Roman church, and his piety carried its errors. He addressed prayers and tender devotion to the Virgin Mary, honouring the creature in ways Scripture reserves for God alone, for there is one Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus. His sacramental and ecclesial framework belonged to a church the Reformation would later weigh by the Word and reform. Applying its rule for figures outside the Reformed tradition, the dictionary honours the insight into the cross and the rigour of his thought while naming the Marian devotion and the Roman setting as the error of his age. The seed of satisfaction he planted, the Reformers brought to full harvest in justification by faith alone.

etymology: From “Eastern” (the Greek-speaking East of the old Roman world) and “Orthodoxy” (Greek orthos, right, and doxa, glory or opinion, “right worship/belief”); the communion of the Eastern churches separated from Rome in the schism of 1054.
biblical_def: Eastern Orthodoxy is the communion of the ancient Eastern churches—Greek, Russian, and others—that broke from Rome in the great schism of 1054. The dictionary weighs it with discrimination, honouring what is true and naming what departs from the Word. To its lasting honour, Eastern Orthodoxy preserved the Trinitarian and Christological orthodoxy of the early church: it confesses the Nicene faith, the full deity and eternal Sonship of Christ, one Person in two natures as defined at Chalcedon, and it treasures the writings of the early fathers and the four great ecumenical councils. For guarding these, the dictionary gives thanks. Yet it names grave departures from Scripture. Orthodoxy practices the veneration of icons—bowing to and kissing images of Christ and the saints—which the second commandment forbids; it teaches a eucharistic doctrine of the real bodily presence in the elements that obscures the finished and sufficient sacrifice of Christ; it gives a place to tradition, councils, and the consensus of the fathers that effectively denies sola scriptura, the supreme and final authority of the written Word; and it invokes the prayers of Mary and the saints, honouring creatures with what belongs to God. The dictionary applies its rule: honour the preserved orthodoxy of the Trinity and the Person of Christ, the reverence and the patristic riches; but name the icon veneration, the eucharistic theology, the inflated authority of tradition, and the invocation of saints as departures that must be reformed by the Word. We rejoice in the faith the East has kept, and call it back from the additions it has made.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is doctrinal and ancient, not the drift of the age. The dictionary first honours what is true: Eastern Orthodoxy guarded the Trinitarian and Christological faith of Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus, and Chalcedon, confessing the full deity and eternal Sonship of Christ and one Person in two natures. It treasures the early fathers and maintains a deep reverence in worship. For preserving the catholic faith of the creeds through the centuries, the dictionary gives genuine thanks, and counts the East a guardian of doctrines we together confess.

Yet grave additions must be named. Orthodoxy venerates icons, bowing to and kissing images of Christ and the saints—the very practice the second commandment forbids, however carefully it distinguishes veneration from worship. It teaches a real bodily presence in the eucharist that clouds the once-for-all, perfect, and finished sacrifice by which Christ hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified. It places tradition, the councils, and the consensus of the fathers on a footing that denies sola scriptura, the supreme authority of the God-breathed written Word. And it invokes Mary and the saints, giving to creatures the mediation that belongs to the one Mediator, Christ Jesus. The dictionary honours the orthodoxy the East has kept and calls it back from the additions it has made, that the faith be measured by the Word alone.

etymology: From Chalcedon, a city in Bithynia opposite Constantinople, where the fourth ecumenical council met in A.D. 451; the name a Greek place-name of uncertain origin.
biblical_def: The Council of Chalcedon was the fourth ecumenical council of the church, assembled in A.D. 451 at Chalcedon to settle the great Christological controversies of the age. Against Eutyches, who confounded the two natures of Christ into one, and building on the orthodoxy of Nicaea, Constantinople, and Ephesus, the council confessed our Lord Jesus Christ to be one and the same Son, perfect in Godhead and perfect in manhood, truly God and truly man—of one substance with the Father as touching His Godhead, and of one substance with us as touching His manhood. It defined that the two natures, the divine and the human, are united in the one Person of the Son “without confusion, without change, without division, without separation,” the distinction of the natures being in no way taken away by the union, but rather the property of each nature preserved and concurring in one Person. The dictionary affirms the Chalcedonian Definition without reservation. It is the church's settled and faithful guard of the great mystery of godliness: God manifest in the flesh. The Word who was God became flesh and dwelt among us, yet did not cease to be God; the Son took to Himself a true body and a reasonable soul, yet His two natures were not mingled into a third thing, nor was the one Person divided into two. Chalcedon fences this truth against every error—against the Eutychian who melts the natures together, the Nestorian who splits the Person, the Arian who denies the Godhead, and the Apollinarian who denies a full humanity. Whoso would know Christ aright must confess Him as Chalcedon confessed Him: one Person, two natures, perfect God and perfect man, the only Mediator between God and men.
webster_summary: The fourth ecumenical council (A.D. 451), which defined our Lord Jesus Christ as one Person in two natures, divine and human, “without confusion, change, division, or separation”; affirmed by the dictionary without reservation.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the errors Chalcedon condemned—monophysitism, Nestorianism, and every denial of Christ's full deity or full humanity—are the corruptions, and the dictionary affirms the council without reservation.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover and to hold fast is the Chalcedonian confession of the one Person of Christ in two natures, divine and human, without confusion, change, division, or separation. The dictionary affirms the council without reservation, as the church's settled and Scriptural guard of the mystery of the incarnation. The errors it condemned are the corruptions to be named: the monophysitism of Eutyches, which melts the two natures into one and so loses either the true Godhead or the true manhood of the Saviour, and the Nestorianism that splits the one Person into two, sundering the natures the Son has joined.

These ancient errors return in every age under new names. Whenever men deny that the Word who was God became truly flesh, or that the flesh He took was a real body and a reasonable soul like ours, or whenever they mingle the natures so that the divine swallows the human, or divide the Person so that the man Jesus is somehow other than the eternal Son, they fall into the very heresies Chalcedon fenced out. The dictionary holds the definition as a fence around the gospel itself, for only a Mediator who is truly God and truly man, in one undivided Person, can reconcile God and men. To confess Christ aright is to confess Him as Chalcedon confessed Him, and the council stands unreservedly affirmed against all who would melt, divide, diminish, or deny.

etymology: Greek Eutyches (“fortunate”); a fifth-century archimandrite of Constantinople whose one-nature teaching gave rise to the monophysite (Eutychian) heresy condemned at Chalcedon.
biblical_def: Eutyches was a fifth-century monk and archimandrite of Constantinople whose teaching on the Person of Christ became the great error condemned at the Council of Chalcedon in A.D. 451. In his zeal against Nestorius, who had divided Christ into two persons, Eutyches over-corrected and confounded the two natures into one: he taught that after the union the manhood of Christ was swallowed up in His deity, as a drop of vinegar in the sea, so that Christ was no longer of one substance with us as touching His manhood. This is the monophysite heresy—from the Greek for “one nature”—and the dictionary names it for what it is: a denial of the true and abiding humanity of the Saviour. Against it Scripture is plain. The Word was made flesh; He took part of the same flesh and blood as the children He came to save; He was made like unto His brethren in all things, sin excepted, that He might be a merciful and faithful High Priest. A Christ whose manhood is dissolved into His Godhead could not have hungered, wept, suffered, died, and risen as a true man, nor could He be the second Adam standing in the place of men. Chalcedon answered Eutyches by confessing one Person in two natures, the divine and the human, united without confusion and without change, the property of each nature preserved. The dictionary marks the Eutychian error as a perennial temptation—the over-reaction that, fearing to divide Christ, ends by diminishing Him. The true confession holds both natures whole and undiminished in the one Person, for our salvation hangs on a Mediator who is fully God and fully man, neither nature lost in the other.
webster_summary: A fifth-century archimandrite of Constantinople whose one-nature (monophysite) teaching dissolved Christ's manhood into His deity; condemned at Chalcedon (A.D. 451), which confessed one Person in two undiminished natures.

corruption_summary: The Eutychian or monophysite error confounds Christ's two natures into one, dissolving His true and abiding humanity into His deity.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the ancient heresy itself, named and rebutted. Eutyches, in zeal against the Nestorian division of Christ into two persons, fell into the opposite ditch and confounded the two natures into one, teaching that after the union the manhood of Christ was swallowed up in His deity. This is monophysitism, the one-nature error, and it is a denial of the true and abiding humanity of the Saviour. The dictionary rebuts it from the plain Word: the children are partakers of flesh and blood, and He likewise took part of the same; in all things it behoved Him to be made like unto His brethren, that He might be a merciful and faithful High Priest.

A Christ whose manhood is dissolved into His Godhead is no Saviour for men. He could not truly hunger, weep, bleed, and die; He could not be the last Adam, made under the law to redeem them that were under the law; the resurrection body He showed His disciples—flesh and bones they might handle—would be an illusion. Chalcedon answered Eutyches by confessing one Person in two natures, the divine and the human, united without confusion and without change, the distinct property of each nature preserved. The dictionary holds this against every age's temptation to so guard the unity of Christ's Person that it diminishes one of His natures. Our salvation hangs on a Mediator fully God and fully man, neither nature lost in the other, both whole and undiminished in the one Lord Jesus Christ.

pos: noun phrase (second-century defenders of the faith)
etymology: From “apologist” (Greek apologia, a reasoned defence); the second- and early-third-century Christian writers—Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, Tertullian, and others—who defended the faith against pagan slander and heresy.
biblical_def: The early apologists were the Christian writers of the second and early third centuries who defended the faith against the slanders of paganism and the corruptions of heresy. Among the chief were Justin Martyr, who reasoned with the philosophers and sealed his witness with his blood; Irenaeus of Lyons, who refuted the Gnostics in Against Heresies and insisted on the apostolic deposit and the rule of faith; Tertullian of Carthage, the fierce Latin advocate who coined much of the church's Trinitarian vocabulary; and others such as Athenagoras and Theophilus. They answered the false charges of atheism, cannibalism, and disloyalty hurled against the Christians, set forth the reasonableness of the faith before emperors and magistrates, and contended for the truth against the Gnostic denial of the Creator, the goodness of the flesh, and the true humanity of Christ. The dictionary honours the early apologists as obeying the apostolic charge to be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh a reason of the hope within them, and as earnestly contending for the faith once delivered unto the saints. They stand as a model of bold, reasoned witness in a hostile world, and Irenaeus especially as an early and valuable guard of the apostolic gospel against heresy. Yet the dictionary weighs them by the Word and not the reverse. Some of the apologists, reasoning with Greek philosophy, leaned too far toward it—Justin's notion of the logos spermatikos conceded too much to the philosophers, and seeds of the later sacramentalism and works-righteousness can be traced among them. They were honourable fathers, not infallible authorities; the dictionary receives their defence of the faith with gratitude while trying every word of theirs by Scripture, the sole and final rule.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The dictionary honours the early apologists for genuine and great labour: they answered the slanders of atheism, cannibalism, and disloyalty hurled at the church, set the reasonableness of the faith before hostile emperors, and contended against the Gnostic heresies that denied the Creator, the goodness of the body, and the true humanity of Christ. Justin reasoned with the philosophers and sealed his witness with martyrdom; Irenaeus guarded the apostolic gospel and the rule of faith; Tertullian forged much of the church's Trinitarian language. They obeyed the charge to be ready always to give an answer, and earnestly contended for the faith once delivered. This is honourable history, received with gratitude.

Yet they must be weighed by the Word, not set above or beside it. Reasoning with Greek thought, some leaned too far toward it: Justin's logos spermatikos, finding seeds of the Word scattered among the pagan philosophers, conceded more to philosophy than Scripture warrants, and the seeds of later sacramentalism and a creeping works-righteousness can be traced among the fathers of this age. The dictionary applies its rule for figures outside the Reformed tradition: receive their defence of the faith and their refutation of heresy with thanks, honour their courage and their orthodoxy on the great matters, but try every word of theirs by Scripture, the sole and final rule. They were faithful fathers, not infallible authorities, and the canon closed at the apostles, not at their successors.

pos: noun phrase (a Byzantine dispute over images)
etymology: From the Greek eikon (image) and klastes (breaker); the eighth- and ninth-century Byzantine dispute between the iconoclasts (image-breakers) and the iconodules (image-venerators) over the use of images in worship.
biblical_def: The Iconoclast Controversy was the long and bitter dispute that shook the Byzantine church in the eighth and ninth centuries over the place of images in Christian worship. On one side stood the iconoclasts—the “image-breakers”—who, beginning under the emperors, condemned the making and venerating of images of Christ and the saints as a breach of the second commandment, and removed or destroyed them. On the other stood the iconodules, the “image-servers,” who defended the veneration of icons, arguing from the incarnation that the invisible God, having taken visible flesh, might now be depicted, and distinguishing the honour given to the image from the worship due to God alone. The Second Council of Nicaea (787) sided with the venerators, and the practice of icon veneration became fixed in the East. The dictionary takes its stand plainly with the iconoclasts on the substance of the matter, though not with every excess of mob and emperor. The second commandment forbids making any graven image or likeness to bow down before it, and the regulative principle of worship holds that God is to be served only as He has appointed in His Word. The bowing to, kissing of, and burning incense before images of Christ and the saints, however the venerators may distinguish veneration from worship, is the very thing Scripture condemns: God is a Spirit, and they that worship Him must worship Him in spirit and in truth, not before the work of men's hands. The argument from the incarnation does not overturn the commandment, for no man hath seen God at any time, and the Son who declared the Father did so in the gospel, not in painted wood. The dictionary honours the iconoclasts' zeal for the holiness of worship and the second commandment, and counts the triumph of image veneration a sad and lasting corruption.
webster_summary: The eighth- and ninth-century Byzantine dispute over images in worship; the dictionary sides with the iconoclasts on the second commandment and the regulative principle, counting the triumph of icon veneration (Second Nicaea, 787) a lasting corruption.

corruption_summary: The triumph of icon veneration at the Second Council of Nicaea (787) fixed in the East a breach of the second commandment; the dictionary stands with the iconoclasts and the regulative principle of worship.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the second commandment and the regulative principle of worship: that God is to be worshipped only as He has appointed in His Word, and that men shall not make any graven image or likeness to bow down before it. The corruption to be named is the veneration of icons that triumphed in the East. The iconodules defended bowing to, kissing, and censing images of Christ and the saints, arguing from the incarnation that the God who took visible flesh may now be depicted, and distinguishing the honour paid to the image from the worship due to God alone. The Second Council of Nicaea in 787 enshrined this practice, and the dictionary judges it a sad and lasting corruption of pure worship.

The dictionary sides with the iconoclasts on the substance, though not with every violence of mob or emperor. The distinction between veneration and worship cannot rescue the practice, for the second commandment forbids the very act of bowing before the likeness, whatever name be given the inward intent. The appeal to the incarnation fails: no man hath seen God at any time, Israel saw no manner of similitude at Horeb lest they corrupt themselves, and the Son declared the Father in the gospel preached, not in painted wood and gilded panel. God is a Spirit, and they that worship Him must worship Him in spirit and in truth. The dictionary honours the iconoclasts' zeal for the holiness of worship, counts the Reformers their heirs in stripping the images from the churches, and holds that the honour of God is guarded only where worship is offered as He commanded, neither more nor less.

etymology: From Anne Hutchinson (1591–1643), an Englishwoman of the Massachusetts Bay Colony whose teaching sparked the Antinomian Controversy of 1636–1638; “Anne” from the Hebrew Hannah (grace).
biblical_def: Anne Hutchinson was an Englishwoman of the Massachusetts Bay Colony whose teaching provoked the Antinomian Controversy of 1636–1638. A woman of evident gifts, sharp mind, and genuine zeal for free grace, she gathered hearers in her home to discuss the sermons and pressed the doctrine of grace against any reliance on works. The dictionary honours what is honourable in her: her earnest love of grace, her recoil from a religion of mere outward duty, and her courage. Yet it must name plainly the errors that the colony's synod and court condemned. She charged most of the ministers with preaching a “covenant of works” rather than a covenant of grace, drifting into antinomianism—the error that so exalts grace as to make the moral law and the fruits of sanctification needless evidence of a true work, when Scripture says faith without works is dead and that by their fruits ye shall know them. More gravely, she claimed direct, immediate revelations of the Spirit apart from and above the written Word, expecting personal voices and impressions to guide her. The dictionary marks this as a breach of two settled truths: cessationism, that the gift of new prophetic revelation ceased with the apostles, and the closed canon, the faith once for all delivered unto the saints, to which nothing is to be added. She also taught and exhorted men publicly in matters of doctrine, against the apostolic order that a woman is not to teach nor usurp authority over the man in the church. The dictionary thus honours her zeal for grace while naming her antinomianism, her claim to private revelation, and her overstepping of the complementarian order as the errors that justly drew the censure of the godly fathers of New England.
webster_summary: The colonial figure (1591–1643) at the centre of the Antinomian Controversy in Massachusetts Bay; honoured for zeal for free grace, but named for antinomianism, claims to immediate private revelation against the closed canon, and overstepping the church's order.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The dictionary honours what is honourable in Anne Hutchinson: a genuine love of free grace, a recoil from a religion of mere outward duty, and real courage. But the principle to recover is the balance her zeal upset. Her antinomianism so exalted grace as to slight the moral law and the necessary fruits of sanctification, charging the ministers with a covenant of works for pressing holiness. Scripture answers that faith without works is dead, and that by their fruits ye shall know them. Free grace does not abolish the law as the rule of the believer's life; it writes the law upon the heart. To love grace and despise the evidences of grace is to misread the gospel she meant to defend.

Two further errors must be named. She claimed direct and immediate revelations of the Spirit—voices and impressions guiding her apart from and above the written Word. The dictionary holds cessationism, that the gift of new prophetic revelation ceased with the apostles, and the closed canon, the faith once for all delivered unto the saints, to which nothing may be added. A spirit that speaks beside the Word is to be tried by the Word and, where it adds to it, refused. And she taught and exhorted men publicly in doctrine, against the apostolic order that a woman is not to teach nor usurp authority over the man in the church. The complementarian order is no slight upon her gifts but the Lord's appointment for His house. The dictionary therefore honours her zeal for grace while naming the antinomianism, the private revelation, and the overstepping of order that justly drew the censure of New England's fathers.

pos: proper noun (an ancient North African city and church centre)
etymology: From the Punic Qart-hadasht (“new city”); the great North African city, refounded as a Roman colony, that became an early centre of Latin Christianity.
biblical_def: Carthage was the great city of Roman North Africa that became, in the second through fifth centuries, a chief centre of Latin-speaking Christianity, home to a vigorous and learned church. From its soil came Tertullian, the fierce apologist who shaped the church's Trinitarian vocabulary; Cyprian, the martyr-bishop who wrote on the unity of the church and the duties of bishops; and, nearby, the towering Augustine of Hippo. The dictionary marks Carthage for the church councils held there, which spoke to two matters of lasting weight. First, the Councils of Carthage (notably 397) listed the books received as canonical Scripture, an early witness to the church's recognition—not creation—of the canon; the church did not give the books their authority but received and acknowledged the authority God had stamped upon them. The dictionary honours this witness while holding that the canon of the Old Testament is the Hebrew Scriptures the Jews received and our Lord confirmed, and that the apocryphal books some African lists included are not inspired Scripture but writings of lesser sort. Second, the African church wrestled with the Donatist schism over the holiness of the church and the validity of sacraments administered by unworthy ministers—a controversy answered by Augustine, that the efficacy of the ordinances rests not on the minister's worth but on God's appointment. The dictionary honours Carthage as a fountain of Latin theology and a faithful early witness to the gospel and the Scriptures, while weighing all its councils and fathers, as ever, by the supreme rule of the written Word.
webster_summary: The great North African city and early centre of Latin Christianity; home to Tertullian and Cyprian, and the site of councils that witnessed to the canon of Scripture and wrestled with the Donatist schism—honoured, yet weighed by the Word.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The dictionary honours Carthage as a fountain of Latin theology and a faithful early witness: home to Tertullian and Cyprian, near to Augustine, and the site of councils that acknowledged the books received as canonical Scripture. The principle to guard here is that the church recognizes the canon, it does not create it. The councils did not confer authority on the Scriptures; they witnessed to the authority God had already stamped upon His inspired Word. Yet some African lists embraced the apocryphal books, which the dictionary, with the Reformers, holds to be writings of lesser sort and not inspired Scripture; the Old Testament canon is the Hebrew Scriptures the Jews received and our Lord confirmed in the law, the prophets, and the psalms.

The African church also faced the Donatist schism, which made the validity of the sacraments and the very being of the church hang upon the worthiness of the minister, so that ordinances administered by the lapsed or unworthy were counted void. Augustine answered rightly that the efficacy of the ordinances rests not on the minister's holiness but on God's appointment, for neither is he that planteth any thing, nor he that watereth, but God that giveth the increase. The dictionary honours the genuine zeal of the African church for purity while naming the Donatist error, and weighs all the councils and fathers of Carthage, as ever, by the supreme and final rule of the written Word.

etymology: Latin columba (“dove”); the name of the sixth-century Irish abbot and missionary (c. 521–597) who founded the monastery of Iona and evangelized the Picts of Scotland.
biblical_def: Columba was a sixth-century Irish abbot and missionary, by tradition of noble birth, who left his native Ireland and crossed the sea to found, about the year 563, the monastery of Iona on a small island off the western coast of Scotland. From that base he and his companions carried the gospel to the Picts of the Scottish mainland and trained a generation of missionaries who spread the faith through Scotland and beyond. The dictionary honours Columba as a labourer in the great commission—a man who forsook home and kindred to preach Christ where He was not named, and who made Iona a lamp of the gospel for the northern peoples. How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace; and how shall they hear without a preacher, and how shall they preach except they be sent? Columba and the Celtic Christianity he represents laboured before the medieval Roman church had fastened its full system upon the West, and the dictionary receives his missionary zeal, his planting of churches, and his training of preachers as honourable and exemplary. It does not pretend he was a Reformed Baptist, nor read back into him the doctrines later recovered at the Reformation; the monastic and sacramental forms of his age belonged to his age. But the substance the dictionary holds up is the apostolic pattern he embodied: a man sent, going to the unreached, preaching the word of the cross, founding congregations, and raising up others to carry the message further. The harvest is great and the labourers few; Columba was one of the few, and the church does well to honour the feet that brought good tidings to the Picts.
webster_summary: The sixth-century Irish missionary (c. 521–597) who founded the monastery of Iona and carried the gospel to the Picts of Scotland; honoured for apostolic missionary labour in obedience to the great commission.
webster_full: COLUMBA, proper noun. [Latin columba, “dove.”] A sixth-century Irish abbot and missionary (c. 521–597).

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is the apostolic missionary pattern Columba embodied, without reading back the medieval forms of his age or the Reformation doctrines recovered later.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover and to honour is the apostolic missionary pattern that Columba embodied. He forsook home and kindred to preach Christ where He was not named, founded Iona as a base for the gospel, carried the word to the Picts of Scotland, and trained others to carry it further. How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings; how shall they hear without a preacher, and how shall they preach except they be sent? Columba was one of the few labourers in a plenteous harvest, and the church does well to give thanks for the feet that brought glad tidings to the northern peoples.

The dictionary marks one care, lest honour become anachronism. Columba was a man of the sixth-century Celtic church, before the medieval Roman system had fastened its full weight upon the West and long before the Reformation recovered the gospel of justification by faith alone. The dictionary does not pretend he was a Reformed Baptist, nor read back into him the doctrines later restored; the monastic and sacramental forms of his age belonged to his age, and where they erred they erred. What it holds up is the substance: a man sent, going to the unreached, preaching the word of the cross, planting congregations, and raising up preachers. That missionary obedience is honourable in every age, and the dictionary commends it without inventing for Columba a churchmanship he did not have.

etymology: Latin Constantinus, from constans (“steadfast, constant”); the Roman emperor (reigned 306–337) who ended the persecution of Christians and summoned the Council of Nicaea.
biblical_def: Constantine was the Roman emperor whose reign marked the great turning of the empire from the persecution of the church toward its favour. The dictionary marks two acts of lasting weight. By the Edict of Milan in 313, Constantine and his co-emperor granted toleration to the Christians, ending the bloody persecutions under which the saints had suffered for nearly three centuries and giving the church liberty to worship openly. And in 325 he summoned and presided over the first ecumenical council, the Council of Nicaea, which against the Arian denial of the Son's deity confessed Christ to be of one substance with the Father, very God of very God. The dictionary honours God's providence in both. The same Lord who turneth the king's heart whithersoever He will, and in whose hand are the kings of the earth, used this emperor to stay the sword from His people and to gather the bishops who guarded the deity of His Son. The dictionary gives thanks for the rest granted the church and for the orthodoxy Nicaea confessed. Yet it names plainly the perils that followed the marriage of church and state begun under Constantine. The favour of emperors brought wealth, power, and worldliness into the church; soon the state would meddle in doctrine, persecute dissenters, and bend the church to imperial ends, and the seeds were sown of a Christendom in which the kingdom of Christ was confounded with the kingdoms of this world. Our Lord's kingdom is not of this world, and the church's weapons are not carnal but mighty through God. The dictionary therefore honours Constantine's providential acts—the peace and the council—while warning that the embrace of Caesar has ever been a more subtle danger to the church's purity than the sword of Caesar.
webster_summary: The Roman emperor (c. 272–337) who ended persecution by the Edict of Milan (313) and summoned the Council of Nicaea (325); honoured for God's providence in both, with the perils of the church-state entanglement that followed named.
webster_full: CONSTANTINE, proper noun. [Latin constans, steadfast.] The Roman emperor (reigned 306–337).

corruption_summary: The marriage of church and state begun under Constantine brought wealth, worldliness, and imperial meddling into the church, sowing the seeds of a Christendom that confounded Christ's kingdom with the kingdoms of this world.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The dictionary first honours God's providence in Constantine's reign. The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD, who turneth it whithersoever He will; by this emperor God ended through the Edict of Milan the long and bloody persecutions under which His saints had suffered, and gave the church liberty to worship openly. And through the Council of Nicaea, which Constantine summoned, God gathered the bishops who confessed His Son to be of one substance with the Father, very God of very God, against the Arian denial. For the rest granted His people and the orthodoxy guarded at Nicaea, the dictionary gives genuine thanks.

Yet the perils that followed must be named. The favour of emperors brought wealth, power, and worldliness into a church that had been purified by suffering; the state soon meddled in doctrine, exiled and persecuted dissenters in the name of Christ, and bent the church to imperial ends. Here were sown the seeds of a Christendom in which the kingdom of the crucified was confounded with the kingdoms of this world. But our Lord said plainly, My kingdom is not of this world, and the weapons of the church's warfare are not carnal but mighty through God. The dictionary honours the providential acts—the peace and the council—while warning that the embrace of Caesar has ever proved a subtler danger to the church's purity than the sword of Caesar, and that the church flourishes by the Word and the Spirit, not by the patronage of princes.
